title: Number of Provinces
description: You are given an n x n matrix isConnected where isConnected[i][j] = 1 if city i and city j are directly connected, and 0 otherwise. A province is a group of directly or indirectly connected cities. Return the total number of provinces.

examples.explanation: Cities 0 and 1 form one province; city 2 forms another.
No cities are connected to each other.

hints: Union every pair of cities with isConnected[i][j] = 1.
Count how many distinct set leaders remain.
DFS/BFS on the matrix works too.

title: Find the Town Judge
description: In a town of n people labeled 1 to n, trust[i] = [a, b] means person a trusts person b. The town judge is a person who trusts nobody and is trusted by everybody else (n - 1 people). Return the label of the town judge, or -1 if there is none. If n = 1 and trust is empty, person 1 is the judge.

examples.explanation: Person 2 is trusted by person 1 and trusts nobody.
Person 3 is trusted by persons 1 and 2 and trusts nobody.

hints: Count for each person how many trust them (in-degree) and how many they trust (out-degree).
The judge has in-degree n-1 and out-degree 0.
One pass over trust fills both counts.

title: Connectivity Queries
description: You are given n nodes labeled 0 to n-1 and a list of undirected edges. Then you are given queries, where each query is [u, v]. For each query, return true if u and v are connected (in the same component) and false otherwise.

examples.explanation: 0 and 2 are connected; 0 and 3 are not; 3 and 4 are connected.
0 and 1 are connected; 1 and 2 are not.

hints: Build the connected components once with Union-Find.
Each query is then just a find(u) == find(v) check.
A node is always connected to itself.

title: Largest Friend Group
description: You are given an n x n matrix isConnected where isConnected[i][j] = 1 if person i and person j are direct friends, and 0 otherwise (friendship is mutual). A friend group is a set of people connected through friendships. Return the size of the largest friend group.

examples.explanation: The largest group is {0, 1} with size 2.
Everyone is alone, so the answer is 1.

hints: Union friends together, then count members per set.
Track the size of each set as you union.
The answer is the maximum set size.

title: Check if Graph is a DAG
description: You are given n nodes labeled 0 to n-1 and a list of directed edges, where each edge [u, v] points from u to v. Return true if the graph is a directed acyclic graph (DAG), i.e. it contains no directed cycle.

examples.explanation: A simple chain has no cycles.
The edges form a directed cycle.

hints: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with in-degree 0.
If every node gets removed, the graph is acyclic.
A self-loop is a cycle of length 1.

title: Can Complete Target Course
description: There are numCourses courses labeled 0 to numCourses-1. prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means you must take course b before course a. Given a target course, return true if the target and all of its (transitive) prerequisites can be completed, i.e. there is no cyclic dependency among them. Courses unrelated to the target do not matter.

examples.explanation: The prerequisite chain 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 has no cycle.
The prerequisites of course 2 contain a cycle.

hints: Follow prerequisite edges starting from the target course.
Use DFS with three colors to detect a cycle in the reachable subgraph.
A cycle anywhere on the target's dependency chain makes it impossible.

title: Cycle Detection with Union-Find
description: You are given n nodes labeled 0 to n-1 and a list of undirected edges that are added one by one in the given order. Return true if adding the edges creates at least one cycle, and false otherwise. A duplicate edge between the same pair of nodes counts as creating a cycle.

examples.explanation: The third edge connects two already-connected nodes.
No cycle is formed.

hints: Process edges in order, unioning their endpoints.
If an edge's endpoints are already in the same set, you found a cycle.
Union-Find detects this in almost-constant time per edge.

title: Find Champion in Tournament
description: In a tournament of n players labeled 0 to n-1, edges[i] = [u, v] means player u defeated player v. A champion is a player who was never defeated by anyone. If there is exactly one champion, return its label; otherwise return -1.

examples.explanation: Player 0 was never defeated.
Both players 0 and 1 were never defeated, so there is no unique champion.

hints: Count how many times each player was defeated (in-degree).
A champion has in-degree 0.
Return -1 unless exactly one player has in-degree 0.

title: Course Schedule
description: There are numCourses courses labeled 0 to numCourses-1. prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means you must take course b before course a. Return true if it is possible to finish all courses, i.e. there is no cyclic dependency.

examples.explanation: Take course 0 first, then course 1.
Courses 0 and 1 depend on each other, so neither can be taken.

hints: Model courses as a directed graph: edge b -> a for prerequisite [a, b].
All courses can be finished exactly when the graph has no cycle.
Use Kahn's algorithm or DFS cycle detection.

title: Course Schedule II
description: There are numCourses courses labeled 0 to numCourses-1. prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means you must take course b before course a. Return any valid order in which all courses can be taken. To keep the answer unique, return the lexicographically smallest valid topological order (at each step pick the smallest-numbered available course). Return an empty array if it is impossible.

examples.explanation: Course 0 has no prerequisites, so it comes first.
The lexicographically smallest valid order is [0,1,2,3].

hints: Kahn's algorithm produces a topological order.
Use a min-heap for the available courses to get the lexicographically smallest order.
If the result has fewer than numCourses courses, return an empty array.

title: Redundant Connection
description: You are given an undirected graph that started as a tree with nodes labeled 1 to n, with one extra edge added. The edges are given in the order they were added. Return the extra edge: the edge that can be removed so the remaining graph is a tree. If several edges qualify, return the one that appears last in the input.

examples.explanation: Removing [2,3] leaves a tree.
Removing [1,4] leaves a tree.

hints: Process edges in order, unioning their endpoints.
The first edge whose endpoints are already connected is the redundant one.
That edge is exactly the one closing a cycle.

title: Network Connections Needed
description: There are n computers labeled 0 to n-1 connected by connections[i] = [a, b]. You can rewire any cable: remove it from its current endpoints and place it between any two disconnected computers. Return the minimum number of rewiring operations needed so all computers are connected, or -1 if it is impossible.

examples.explanation: One redundant cable can be moved to connect computer 3.
Two cables must be moved to connect computers 4 and 5.

hints: Count the connected components with Union-Find.
You need (components - 1) cables to connect everything.
A cable is reusable only if it is redundant: count edges that union already-connected nodes.

title: Satisfiability of Equality Equations
description: You are given an array of equations, each of the form "a==b" or "a!=b" where a and b are lowercase letters. Return true if it is possible to assign integers to the variables so that all equations hold, and false otherwise.

examples.explanation: a cannot be both equal and unequal to b.
Assign the same integer to a and b.

hints: First union all variables linked by ==.
Then check every != equation: its sides must be in different sets.
A statement like "a!=a" is immediately false.

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
description: You are given points[i] = [xi, yi] on a 2D plane. The cost of connecting points i and j is the Manhattan distance |xi - xj| + |yi - yj|. Return the minimum total cost to connect all points (the cost of a minimum spanning tree).

examples.explanation: The MST has total cost 20.
The MST has total cost 18.

hints: Build the complete graph with Manhattan edge weights.
Run Kruskal's algorithm: sort edges, union greedily.
Prim's algorithm starting from any point also works.

title: Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column
description: You are given stones[i] = [xi, yi] on a 2D plane. You may remove a stone if it shares its row or column with another stone that has not been removed yet. Return the maximum number of stones you can remove.

examples.explanation: Remove 5 stones, leaving 1.
Remove 3 stones, leaving 2.

hints: Stones sharing a row or column belong to the same group.
Union each stone's row-id with its column-id.
From each connected group of k stones you can remove k-1 stones.

title: Minimum Score of a Path Between Two Cities
description: There are n cities labeled 1 to n connected by roads[i] = [u, v, distance]. The score of a path is the minimum distance among the roads on that path. Return the minimum possible score among all paths from city 1 to city n.

examples.explanation: Path 1-4 has score 7; path 1-2-4 has score min(9,5) = 5, which is smaller.
Walks may revisit nodes, so every road reachable from city 1 counts; the smallest distance among them is 2 (walk 1-2-1-3-4).

constraints: There is at least one path from 1 to n
hints: Because walks may revisit nodes, only the connected component of city 1 matters.
The answer is the minimum road distance inside that component.
Union all roads while tracking the minimum edge weight per set.

title: Redundant Connection II
description: You are given a directed graph that started as a rooted tree with n nodes labeled 1 to n, with one extra directed edge added. Return that extra edge: the edge whose removal leaves a valid rooted tree. If a node has two parents, consider the two candidate edges in input order and remove the later one if the remaining graph is a valid tree, otherwise remove the earlier one. If no node has two parents, return the edge that closes the directed cycle.

examples.explanation: Node 3 has two parents; removing the later edge [2,3] leaves a tree.
No node has two parents; [4,1] closes the cycle.

hints: First check whether some node has two parents.
If so, test removing the later edge: the rest must be a tree with n-1 edges.
Otherwise the extra edge is the one that closes a cycle (plain redundant connection).

title: Alien Dictionary
description: Words are sorted lexicographically in an alien language whose alphabet order is unknown. Given the sorted list of words (lowercase letters), derive the alphabet order: return a string containing each distinct letter exactly once such that every word's letters respect the order. If several orders are valid, return the lexicographically smallest one. Return an empty string if no valid order exists (a cycle, or a longer word appearing before its own prefix).

examples.explanation: The derived order is "wertf".
z comes before x.

constraints: words is sorted in the alien order
hints: Compare adjacent words: the first differing letters give an ordering edge.
Build the graph and run Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap for the smallest order.
Watch for the invalid prefix case and for cycles.

title: Couples Holding Hands
description: There are n couples (2n people) labeled 0 to 2n-1, where people (2i, 2i+1) form a couple. They sit in a row given by row[i]. In one swap you may swap any two people. Return the minimum number of swaps so that every couple sits side by side (in adjacent seats 2k, 2k+1 for some k).

examples.explanation: Swap person 1 with person 2 to get [0,1,2,3].
Couples (2,3) and (0,1) already sit together.

hints: Think of each seat-pair as needing its two couples to be united.
Union the couple-ids sitting in each adjacent pair.
A group of k couples needs k-1 swaps: answer = couples - groups.

title: Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in MST
description: You are given n vertices labeled 0 to n-1 and edges[i] = [u, v, w]. An edge is critical if it appears in every MST; it is pseudo-critical if it appears in some but not every MST. Return [critical, pseudoCritical], where each is the list of edge indices (as given in the input) in ascending order.

examples.explanation: Edges 0 and 1 are in every MST; edges 2,3,4,5 appear in some MST.
No edge is in every MST; each appears in some MST.

hints: Compute the MST weight once with Kruskal.
An edge is critical if removing it increases the MST weight.
An edge is pseudo-critical if forcing it in keeps the MST weight unchanged.
